newsitem.title: USA: Floodwaters spread as Red River dike breaks.
newsitem.headline: Floodwaters spread as Red River dike breaks.

text.p: Several thousand people were evacuated in the Red River valley after dozens of houses were flooded by swollen waters that breached a dike in Fargo, officials said Friday.

The river burst through a section of temporary earthen dike Thursday evening, flooding a school and 20 homes in old Fargo. Witnesses said it looked like a "tidal wave," but there were no reports of injuries.
"Those homes are now in the river," Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness told Reuters.
Radio reports said 1,000 people had been evacuated from the area. CNN reported that the National Guard was called in to evacuate residents of Oakport Township in Minnesota.
In Grand Forks, 75 miles downstream, officials said 1,000 people had been evacuated as water levels continued to rise.
Volunteers struggled throughout the night to buttress clay dikes in Grand Forks where the river rose to 51.77 feet early Friday, surpassing the previous record of 50 feet set in 1897.
The National Weather Service said it expected the river to crest at 52 feet Friday night or early Saturday. Flood stage in Grand Forks is 28 feet.
Mayor Furness said Fargo may have seen the worst of the flood and the Red River appeared to be holding there at 39.55 feet.
But in Grand Forks authorities issued a mandatory evacuation for approximately 690 homes in low-lying residential areas amid concern that dikes might not hold.
The National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning for parts of the town, signalling that flooding was probably imminent.

"We have no major breach in the dike at this time, but we feel they are suspect. We're doing this as a purely precautionary measure," Byron Sieber, spokesman for the Grand Forks Emergency Operations Center, said about the evacuation.
Grand Forks Mayor Pat Owens ordered schools and all non-emergency businesses closed Friday as a precaution, and she urged all available volunteers to help fill sandbags.
"This is probably a disaster of more magnitude than any of us will ever see in our lifetime," Owens said.
